title: Peterke
lines: Once there was a poor man.
This poor man had as many children as a sieve has holes, and one more.
The poor fellow did not even know whom to ask to be godfather to his newborn son,
because even the priest and the cantor were already godfathers to his children.
Oh, what a poor world, what a hard bed!
So the poor man set off with many sighs to look for a godfather.
By evening he reached a great forest, and he got so lost in it
that he could not find his way out at all.
He wandered this way and that, and all at once he met a tiny little man,
whose beard was two yards long and dragged along the ground behind him.
The poor man was frightened,
for he had never in all his life seen such a strange creature.
The tiny man spoke to him:
"What are you doing here, friend?
What is your business?"
The poor man was even more frightened.
"Well, this must be the devil," he thought to himself,
"and he will take me down, God knows where!"
He answered him:
"Oh, my dear tiny little man, my life and death are in your hands.
I set out to look for a godfather, because I have as many children
as a sieve has holes, and one more; the priest is already a godfather to them,
and the cantor too; not a single soul will agree to be a godfather."
The tiny man said:
"Do not fret over that! I will be that child's godfather!
I ask only one thing: when he is seven years, seven months,
seven weeks and seven days old, give the boy to me, and I will take good care of him."
The poor man agreed.
He thought God had given him plenty of children; one given away would hardly be missed.
With that they turned around and went to the poor man's house,
and the child was baptised Peter.
His godfather at once bought him such baby clothes
that not even the king's child had finer ones.
Well, time went by.
All at once Peterke's parents noticed
that the time was nearly up when they had to give their child to the tiny man.
Oh! The poor man shed many bitter tears,
but his wife shed even more; they grieved and sighed a great deal
over why they had to part with this dear child of their hearts,
for there was no child so handsome, with black hair and black eyes, so clever-handed,
so wise as he was.
But all their grieving was in vain, in vain they shed so many bitter tears,
Peterke became seven years, seven months,
seven weeks and seven days old, and he had to be taken to his godfather.
The poor man said to his wife:
"Well, wife, bake me a cake in the ashes. The time has come,
what I promised seven years ago, I cannot take back!"
The poor woman cried, she cried bitterly, but she baked the cake all the same,
got her husband ready for the road, and he took Peterke away.
They walked and walked, and by evening they reached the great forest.
When they were deep inside, the earth opened before them, and out popped the tiny man.
He did not even let the poor man speak; he snatched Peterke from him,
and through the opening he had come out of, he vanished with him.
And the poor man set off home in great sorrow.
For fourteen whole days the tiny man carried his godson downwards,
and on the fourteenth day they reached a meadow
where golden grass grew, diamond flowers bloomed and golden horses grazed.
But, so I don't mix up my words, by then Peterke had grown into a fine, big lad.
For three days they went on through this land, across golden meadows everywhere,
through golden forests and past golden fish ponds.
On the third day they came to a castle that turned on a diamond leg.
Here the tiny man struck the castle gate with a golden rod,
the gate opened at once, and he himself turned a somersault over his head,
and lo, he became a young lady so wonderfully beautiful
that you could look at the sun, but not at her.
Peter could not say a word; he was so amazed he could not speak.
Then the beautiful young lady said:
"Listen, handsome lad!
A wicked old witch put a curse on me that I should be a tiny man
until I found a bridegroom seven years, seven months, seven weeks and seven days old.
Now I have found you, and if you will have me, look, do you see this fine kingdom?
It will all be yours!"
And Peterke had not a single word against that.
At once they harnessed six diamond-haired horses to a diamond coach,
drove up in a moment to Peter's family, brought down his father,
his mother and all his brothers and sisters to the land of happiness,
there they held a great feast, and they are still alive today, if they have not died.
